section.title: The Olivet Discourse: Judgment Parables
section.sectionRationale: The discourse ends with three parables of the coming judgment. The ten virgins call for readiness that cannot be borrowed at the last minute; the talents call for faithful, fruitful stewardship until the Master returns; and the sheep and goats reveal the final separation of all nations before the enthroned Son of Man.
section.thesis: Because the Son of Man will surely come to judge, His people must be ready with a readiness no one else can supply, must invest what He entrusts rather than bury it in fear, and must show the reality of their faith by mercy to the least, for how they treat His brothers they treat Him.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the parable of the ten virgins; the parable of the talents; and the judgment of the sheep and the goats.

verses.text: “At that time the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom.
Five of them were foolish, and five were wise.
The foolish ones took their lamps but did not take along any extra oil.
But the wise ones took oil in flasks along with their lamps.
When the bridegroom was delayed, they all became drowsy and fell asleep.
At midnight the cry rang out: ‘Here is the bridegroom! Come out to meet him!’
Then all the virgins woke up and trimmed their lamps.
The foolish ones said to the wise, ‘Give us some of your oil; our lamps are going out.’
‘No,’ said the wise ones, ‘or there may not be enough for both us and you. Instead, go to those who sell oil and buy some for yourselves.’
But while they were on their way to buy it, the bridegroom arrived. Those who were ready went in with him to the wedding banquet, and the door was shut.
Later the other virgins arrived and said, ‘Lord, lord, open the door for us!’
But he replied, ‘Truly I tell you, I do not know you.’
Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour.
For it is just like a man going on a journey, who called his servants and entrusted them with his possessions.
To one he gave five {{talanton|talents}}, to another two talents, and to another one talent, each according to his own ability. And he went on his journey.
The servant who had received the five talents went at once and put them to work and gained five more.
Likewise, the one with the two talents gained two more.
But the servant who had received the one talent went off, dug a hole in the ground, and hid his master’s money.
After a long time the master of those servants returned and settled accounts with them.
The servant who had received the five talents came and presented five more. ‘Master,’ he said, ‘you entrusted me with five talents. See, I have gained five more.’
His master replied, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant! You have been faithful with a few things; I will put you in charge of many things. Enter into the joy of your master!’
The servant who had received the two talents also came and said, ‘Master, you entrusted me with two talents. See, I have gained two more.’
His master replied, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant! You have been faithful with a few things; I will put you in charge of many things. Enter into the joy of your master!’
Finally, the servant who had received the one talent came and said, ‘Master, I knew that you are a hard man, reaping where you have not sown and gathering where you have not scattered seed.
So I was afraid and went out and hid your talent in the ground. See, you have what belongs to you.’
‘You wicked, lazy servant!’ replied his master. ‘You knew that I reap where I have not sown and gather where I have not scattered seed.
Then you should have deposited my money with the bankers, and on my return I would have received it back with interest.
Therefore take the talent from him and give it to the one who has ten talents.
For everyone who has will be given more, and he will have an abundance. But the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him.
And throw that worthless servant into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’

units.label: The sheep and the goats
units.note: as you did to the least, you did to Me

verses.text: When the Son of Man comes in His glory, and all the angels with Him, He will sit on His glorious throne.
All the nations will be gathered before Him, and He will separate the people one from another, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats.
He will place the sheep on His right and the goats on His left.
Then the King will say to those on His right, ‘Come, you who are blessed by My Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.
For I was hungry and you gave Me something to eat, I was thirsty and you gave Me something to drink, I was a stranger and you took Me in,
I was naked and you clothed Me, I was sick and you looked after Me, I was in prison and you visited Me.’
Then the righteous will answer Him, ‘Lord, when did we see You hungry and feed You, or thirsty and give You something to drink?
When did we see You a stranger and take You in, or naked and clothe You?
When did we see You sick or in prison and visit You?’
And the King will reply, ‘Truly I tell you, whatever you did for one of the {{elachistos|least}} of these brothers of Mine, you did for Me.’
Then He will say to those on His left, ‘Depart from Me, you who are cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.
For I was hungry and you gave Me nothing to eat, I was thirsty and you gave Me nothing to drink,
I was a stranger and you did not take Me in, I was naked and you did not clothe Me, I was sick and in prison and you did not look after Me.’
And they too will reply, ‘Lord, when did we see You hungry or thirsty or a stranger or naked or sick or in prison, and did not minister to You?’
Then the King will answer, ‘Truly I tell you, whatever you did not do for one of the least of these, you did not do for Me.’
And they will go away into {{aionios|eternal}} punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.”

talanton.gloss: A talent, a very large sum of money, about twenty years' wages for a laborer. In the parable it stands for whatever the Master entrusts to His servants, gifts, resources, opportunities, the gospel itself, to be invested for Him, not buried in fear.

elachistos.gloss: Least, smallest, most insignificant. The King identifies Himself with the least of these, the hungry, the stranger, the sick, the imprisoned; how one treats them reveals the heart's true response to Him, for in serving them one serves Him.

aionios.gloss: Eternal, everlasting, belonging to the age to come. The same word describes both the punishment of the cursed and the life of the righteous; the two destinies are of equal, unending duration, and the judgment is final.

basic.context: Jesus closes the discourse with three parables about His return and judgment. Ten virgins wait for a bridegroom; five bring extra oil and are ready, five do not and are shut out. A master entrusts talents to three servants; two invest and are rewarded, one buries his in fear and is condemned. Finally the Son of Man gathers all nations and separates sheep from goats, welcoming those who served Him in the hungry, the stranger, the sick, and the prisoner, and rejecting those who did not, for as they treated the least, they treated Him.
basic.hermeneutics: The three parables build on the call to watch: readiness, faithfulness, and mercy. The oil pictures a real preparedness that cannot be borrowed or faked at the last moment. The talents warn against fearful passivity; faith works. The sheep and goats show that genuine faith bears the fruit of love; the deeds do not earn salvation but reveal it.
basic.originalLanguages: The master entrusts talanta, talents, huge sums, to be invested. The King identifies with the elachistoi, the least, so that serving them is serving Him. And the two destinies are both aionios, eternal, unending life or unending punishment.
basic.typology: The bridegroom and the wedding banquet fulfill the prophetic image of God as husband and the messianic marriage supper. The Son of Man enthroned to judge the nations fulfills Daniel 7. The Shepherd separating sheep from goats echoes Ezekiel 34.
basic.christ: Jesus is the delayed but certain Bridegroom, the returning Master who settles accounts, and the enthroned Son of Man and King who judges all nations. He is the King so united with His people that kindness to the least is kindness to Him.
basic.god: God prepared the kingdom for the blessed from the foundation of the world and the eternal fire for the devil and his angels. He rewards faithful stewardship, welcomes mercy done to the least, and justly judges fruitless, loveless unbelief.
basic.crossReferences: Ezekiel 34 pictures God separating the sheep. Daniel 7 gives the Son of Man enthroned. Luke 19 parallels the parable of the pounds. James 2 teaches that faith without works is dead.
basic.oneStory: The last discourse ends by fixing the disciples' eyes on the judgment that closes history: the Bridegroom comes, the Master returns, the King is enthroned. Between now and then, His people are to be ready, faithful, and merciful. The story of the kingdom will reach its consummation when the Son of Man separates all humanity, welcoming His own into the joy of their Master and the kingdom prepared from the foundation of the world.

context.literary:
Chapter 25 is the second half of the Olivet Discourse and is tied to chapter 24 by the little word 'then' and by the repeated command to keep watch. The last verse of the previous section already set a servant at his master's door, 24:45-51, and the three scenes here widen that single servant into three pictures of the same waiting: a wedding party, a business trust and a court of the nations. Together they answer the question 'what should we be doing until He comes?'

The three scenes are built in a deliberate order. The ten virgins ask about readiness, the talents ask about faithful work, and the sheep and goats ask about love shown to Christ's people. Each begins with something held in common that is then divided: ten virgins become five and five, three servants become two who invest and one who buries, and all the nations become sheep and goats. In each, the dividing line is invisible until the master arrives. In each, the worst fate is a closed door, an outer darkness or an eternal fire.

The scenes also change in kind. The first two are parables that Jesus introduces with 'the kingdom of heaven will be like' and 'it is just like.' The third begins as an apocalyptic scene, 'when the Son of Man comes in His glory,' and uses only one picture, the shepherd, to describe the separation. The effect is that the discourse ends not in a story but in the throne room itself. It is the last of the five great discourses and the final public word before the passion, and its closing line, 'eternal life,' 25:46, completes the arc that began with the disciples' question about the end of the age, 24:3.

Within the parables there are matching patterns of speech. Both the virgins and the lazy servant speak to a master and are answered with a verdict about their identity, 'I do not know you,' 'You wicked, lazy servant.' The sheep and goats both ask 'when did we see You?' and are both answered by the King. Each parable is built on a surprise that shows what was truly in the heart.
context.historical:
The wedding scene in verses 1 to 13 reflects the customs of a Jewish village wedding as best we can reconstruct them. The bridegroom went to the bride's house and then led the party in procession to his own home for the feast. Bridesmaids waited with lamps to light the way and to greet him, and since the exact hour could not be fixed, delays were normal. Shutting the door once the company was inside protected the feast and marked the end of admission. The lamps may have been oil lamps or torches wrapped with oil-soaked cloth, and either way they needed fuel to last through a long night.

The talents in verses 14 to 30 were not coins but a weight of silver, and the size of the sum is the point. A talent was worth about six thousand denarii, and since a day labourer earned about one denarius a day, one talent was something like twenty years of wages. Even the servant who got one was entrusted with a fortune. Servants in the ancient household were often given large responsibility for their master's property, and the master's absence for a long journey was a common reality for estate owners. The servant's excuse, that he buried the money, was also sensible by ancient standards, since burying valuables was a recognised way of keeping them safe. The master's reply that he should at least have used the bankers reflects the practice of deposit banking with interest.

The picture of a shepherd who separates sheep from goats in verse 32 comes from the pastoral life of Palestine. Sheep and goats often grazed in a single mixed flock, and a shepherd could tell them apart and sort them when the time came. A mixed herd with a difference that only the shepherd's eye settles is the image Jesus chose for the nations.

A first hearer familiar with Daniel would also hear in the scene the court of Daniel 7 and the gathering of the nations of Joel 3. The acts of mercy listed in verses 35 and 36, feeding the hungry, welcoming strangers, clothing the naked, visiting the sick and the imprisoned, were recognised duties in Jewish piety, and they echo what the prophets said true religion looks like, Isaiah 58:6-7.
context.canonical:
The bridegroom image is an old one. The prophets speak of God as Israel's husband, Isaiah 54:5 and Hosea 2:19-20, and Isaiah 62:5 says, 'as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you.' Jesus has already used the image of Himself, answering the question about fasting with 'the guests of the bridegroom,' 9:15, and John the Baptist called himself the bridegroom's friend, John 3:29. The marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:7-9, is the same feast seen from the end.

The talents belong with the parable of the minas in Luke 19:11-27, which is similar but told in a different setting, near Jerusalem to people who thought the kingdom would appear at once. Where Luke has ten servants each given the same sum, Matthew has three given different sums according to their ability, and the point shifts from equal opportunity to proportionate faithfulness. The principle 'everyone who has will be given more' also appears at 13:12 and in Luke 8:18.

The scene of the nations drawn before the Son of Man draws on Daniel 7:9-14 and Joel 3:1-3, where the LORD gathers the nations to judge them for the way they treated His people. Ezekiel 34:17-22 supplies the shepherd who judges between sheep and goats. The test of care for the weak echoes Proverbs 19:17, Isaiah 58, Ezekiel 18:7 and Job 31, and the words of the King recall Matthew 10:40-42, where welcoming Christ's messengers is welcoming Him, and 18:5.

The New Testament holds all three parables together. Paul reminds believers that all must appear before the judgment seat of Christ, 2 Corinthians 5:10, and that each will give an account to God, Romans 14:10-12. James insists that faith without works is dead, James 2:14-17, and John asks how God's love can remain in someone who sees a brother in need and refuses help, 1 John 3:17-18. Revelation 20:11-15 gives the great white throne, and Revelation 3:3 echoes the thief image of the previous chapter.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew's readers were a community in the long middle of the story, past the resurrection and not yet at the return. They needed a reason to keep going, and they needed to know that the delay did not mean the promise had failed. The ten virgins say that the delay is real, that everyone will grow drowsy in it, and that what counts is whether there is oil. The talents say that the delay is a trust, an opportunity to work with what has been given. The sheep and goats say that the judgment is not an abstraction but is focused on how people have treated the Lord's own.

Matthew also wants his readers to be shaken out of any comfort that comes from proximity to Jesus. The five foolish virgins call Him 'Lord, lord,' just as the false disciples do in 7:21-23, and the goats call Him 'Lord' too. Nothing in the language of discipleship, by itself, secures the verdict. The sign of genuine discipleship is a readiness and a way of life that has been formed by the master's own character.

At the same time the discourse is a word of hope. The faithful are not told to fear the master but to share his joy, 25:21, 23. The kingdom was 'prepared for you from the foundation of the world,' verse 34. For people facing persecution, hunger and prison themselves, the identification of Christ with the least of these meant that no suffering of theirs went unseen.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The three scenes are parables and a judgment vision, and they describe what the final day will be like. They are not instructions for how to run a household, a business or a court. The details of the parable, such as the wise virgins refusing to share their oil or the master harvesting where he did not sow, are not endorsements. The master's harshness is the servant's own accusation, and the master answers it by turning the argument back on him, 25:26-27. We are not told that God is a hard man.

What does carry over is the purpose of each parable. Be ready. Use what you have been given. Treat the needy as if they were Christ Himself. The last of these is an instruction as well as a warning, and it is not tied to special circumstances, since 'the least of these' will be present until He comes. The parable does not say that good works earn the kingdom. The righteous are surprised, which shows they were not counting. It does say that a faith that never reaches the hungry, the stranger and the prisoner is not the faith that the King recognises.

debates.question: What is the oil in the parable of the ten virgins?

views.label: Genuine faith or a real relationship with Christ
views.case: The wise and foolish both have lamps and both sleep. What separates them is something inward that cannot be borrowed in the last minute. This matches the 'Lord, lord' of 7:21-23 and the closing 'I do not know you,' which says the problem was never external, since all ten looked alike.

views.label: The Holy Spirit
views.case: Oil is a regular symbol of the Spirit's anointing, as in the anointing of kings and priests, 1 Samuel 16:13. On this reading the foolish had the outward form without the Spirit's life, and Paul's statement that anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to Him, Romans 8:9, is the parallel.

views.label: Good works or a life of obedience
views.case: The lamps are said to shine, and Matthew 5:16 speaks of letting your light shine so that people see your good works. On this reading the oil is the visible fruit that keeps the light burning, and it fits the parables that follow.

debates.bearing: Jesus does not identify the oil, and He builds the story so that the point is clear without it. The one thing the oil cannot be is something that can be passed from one person to another. Each must have their own, and each must have it before the midnight cry.

debates.question: Who are 'the least of these brothers of Mine'?

views.label: Anyone in need
views.case: The list is of universal human needs: hunger, thirst, strangers, nakedness, sickness and prison. On this reading Christ identifies Himself with all suffering people, and the judgment is about whether nations and individuals showed mercy. This was the dominant view in the church through much of history and is widely held now.

views.label: Disciples of Jesus, especially those who suffer for Him
views.case: In Matthew, 'brothers' are those who do the Father's will, 12:48-50, and 28:10, and 'little ones' means disciples, 10:42 and 18:6. The nations are judged by how they received the messengers of the gospel, as in 10:40-42, and the list matches the sufferings of persecuted missionaries. Hebrews 2:11 says that Jesus is not ashamed to call believers brothers.

views.label: The Jewish people
views.case: A smaller group of interpreters takes the brothers as Israel, and reads the scene in light of Joel 3, where the nations are judged by their treatment of God's people. This has the benefit of fitting the prophetic background but is the least common reading in Matthew's own usage.

debates.bearing: The second reading has strong support in Matthew's own vocabulary, but the first sets no limit on mercy, and the text never discourages us from caring for anyone. In either reading the lesson is the same: nothing done to a person in Christ's name or in His image is lost to Him.

debates.question: Does this scene teach that people are saved by their works?

views.label: The works are the evidence of faith
views.case: The King welcomes the righteous 'blessed by My Father,' verse 34, and the kingdom is something they inherit. They are surprised by their own deeds, which suggests the deeds flowed from a changed heart rather than from calculation. Paul and James both teach that justification is by faith and that living faith bears fruit, Ephesians 2:8-10, James 2:14-17.

views.label: The works are the actual criterion
views.case: Some read the passage as stating plainly that the final verdict follows conduct, which is what Romans 2:6-7 also says, that God will repay each person according to what they have done. On this view Matthew holds grace and judgment according to works together without trying to reconcile them.

debates.bearing: The passage does not call people to earn a place but to see that no one will be able to claim faith while ignoring Christ's people. Even those who read the works as a criterion agree that the works are what the King's own grace produces.

study.originalLanguages:
The wise and foolish virgins are contrasted with the words phronimos and moros, 25:2. They are the same pair that Jesus used in the Sermon on the Mount for the two builders, 7:24-26. The wise man heard and acted; the foolish man heard and did not. The parable is therefore not about cleverness, since all ten had a lamp and all ten slept. It is the old distinction between hearing and doing, now set in the light of the Bridegroom's return. The cry of the foolish virgins at the door, 'Lord, lord,' kyrie kyrie, echoes 7:21, and the verdict 'I do not know you,' ouk oida hymas, echoes 7:23, 'I never knew you,' oudepote egnon. The door is shut, ekleisthe he thyra, a passive verb: the closing is simply done, and no pleading can undo it.

The word talanton in verses 15 to 28 originally meant a weight, and by Jesus' day it named a very large sum of silver. The English word 'talent' for a natural gift comes from this parable and not the other way round. The master gives 'each according to his own ability,' dynamis, which means power or capacity, so the trust is matched to the servant. The first two servants 'put them to work,' ergasato, and 'gained,' ekerdesen, and the master's praise is word for word the same for both, 'Well done, good and faithful servant,' verses 21 and 23. Faithfulness, not the amount, is what earns the verdict. The third servant is called poneros and oknēros, 'wicked and lazy,' and later achreios, 'worthless,' literally 'useless,' verse 30. He is condemned for what he did not do, which is the sin of omission. The bankers, trapezitai, are the table-men who dealt in money. The outer darkness, to skotos to exoteron, appears also in 8:12 and 22:13, and the weeping and gnashing of teeth in 8:12, 13:42, 13:50, 22:13, 24:51 and here, so that the phrase is Matthew's regular marker of final exclusion.

In the third scene the nations are ethne, a word that in Matthew can mean Gentiles, as in 10:5, or all peoples, as in 28:19. The shepherd separates probata, sheep, from eriphoi, kids or young goats. The words that carry the weight are in verses 34 and 41. The sheep are 'blessed by My Father,' hoi eulogemenoi tou patros mou, and the kingdom is 'prepared,' hetoimasmenen, 'for you from the foundation of the world.' The goats are simply 'cursed,' kateramenoi, not 'cursed by My Father,' and the eternal fire is prepared, using the same verb, 'for the devil and his angels,' not for people. The text itself does not give the two destinies parallel origins. Hell is not what God made humanity for.

The phrase 'the least of these,' elachistos, is the superlative of mikros, small. In verses 35 and 36 the strangers are 'taken in,' synagagete, literally gathered in, and the sick and prisoners are 'looked after' or 'visited,' episkeptomai, a verb meaning to look in on with care. The unusually repeated lists in verses 35 to 36, 37 to 39, 42 to 43 and 44 are Matthew's way of letting the words of mercy linger.

The last word of the discourse is aionios, 'eternal,' applied to both punishment, kolasis, and life, zoe, in verse 46. The same adjective modifies both nouns, so whatever is true of the duration of one is true of the other. Matthew's word for the punishment, kolasis, means penalty or chastisement, and the only other place it appears in the New Testament is 1 John 4:18, where fear is said to have to do with it.

typology.type: The Bridegroom and the wedding banquet
typology.fulfillment: The prophets spoke of God as husband to His people, Isaiah 54:5 and Isaiah 62:5, and as the one who will betroth her to Himself forever, Hosea 2:19-20. Jesus takes the title when He speaks of the bridegroom being 'taken' from His disciples, 9:15, and when He tells this parable. The correspondence is that the divine husband has come in person, and His coming means a feast. The escalation is that the marriage is no longer a metaphor for Israel alone but is the union of Christ with His church, Ephesians 5:25-27, which ends in 'the marriage supper of the Lamb,' Revelation 19:7-9. The type falls short in one detail. In this parable the ten are the bridegroom's attendants and not the bride, so the parable teaches readiness and does not set out the church as bride; Ephesians 5 and Revelation 19 do that.

typology.type: The delayed master and the faithful steward
typology.fulfillment: Scripture often shows a leader who goes away and a people tested by his absence. When Moses was long in coming down from Sinai, the people made a calf, Exodus 32:1. The parable shows the same test at a larger scale: the departure of the Lord and the long delay show what His servants do with what they have been given. The correspondence is delay as a test of fidelity. The escalation is that the Master who leaves will return in person to a household that already knows His character, and the rewards are 'many things' and 'the joy of your master.' The pattern falls short in that Moses came down to a failure and burned the calf, while the returning Master will reward the faithful before He judges the rest.

typology.type: The Shepherd who judges between sheep and goats, Ezekiel 34
typology.fulfillment: In Ezekiel, the LORD condemns the shepherds who have fed themselves and promises, 'I will judge between one sheep and another, between the rams and the goats,' Ezekiel 34:17. He promises to set one shepherd over them, 34:23. Jesus takes the shepherd's role in verse 32, and the 'rams and goats' of Ezekiel become the sheep and goats of the nations. The correspondence includes the key charge: the strong sheep trampled the pasture and muddied the water that the weak needed, Ezekiel 34:18-19, which matches the goats' neglect of the needy. The escalation is that Ezekiel's judgment is within Israel, while Jesus' is of every nation, and the shepherd is not merely like the LORD but is the Son of Man enthroned.

typology.type: The Son of Man enthroned over the nations, Daniel 7 and Joel 3
typology.fulfillment: Daniel saw one like a son of man given dominion over 'the people of every nation and language,' Daniel 7:14, and Joel pictured the LORD gathering all nations for judgment, Joel 3:2. Verses 31 and 32 combine the two, with the Son of Man on His glorious throne and all the nations gathered before Him. The correspondence is complete in the throne and the nations. The escalation is the identification: the King who judges has been hungry, thirsty, a stranger, naked, sick and in prison, and He judges by what was done to Him in those who bear His name. The type falls short of the revelation because neither Daniel nor Joel names the criterion of judgment, which Jesus reveals here.

study.christ:
This chapter shows Christ in three roles, and in each of them He is at the centre of the scene rather than a bystander. In the first He is the Bridegroom, in the second the Master, in the third the King. Each title is Old Testament language that points to God, and Jesus uses each of them for Himself without hesitation.

The Bridegroom is the sure and delayed arrival. The parable says He was 'delayed,' and it does not say He forgot. The cry at midnight, 'Here is the bridegroom!' verse 6, is the announcement that the waiting is over. It is the gospel in the form of an arrival. The door that opens for the ready closes behind them, and those inside are with Him at the feast. Nothing in the parable pictures the Bridegroom as a threat to the ready. For them His coming is joy, as John the Baptist said of Himself as the friend of the bridegroom, John 3:29. The warning is for the unready alone.

The Master is the one who entrusts, who is absent, and who returns to settle accounts. The talents are His, not ours. What He gives He gives to servants who are to work for Him, and what He praises He praises in His own language: 'good and faithful servant.' His promise is generous beyond the work, 'Enter into the joy of your master,' verses 21 and 23. This is the same Lord who 'came not to be served but to serve,' 20:28, and who will gird Himself to serve those who are watching when He returns, Luke 12:37. The servant who feared Him misjudged Him, calling him hard, and in the end he was judged by his own estimate. The portrait of Christ that the lazy servant had was false, and it is false because he never took the trouble to know the Master.

The King is the most striking portrait, because He is the glorious Son of Man on His throne and, in the same breath, the one who was hungry and a stranger. 'Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers of Mine, you did for Me,' verse 40. This is the doctrine of the incarnation turned into the principle of judgment. He took on flesh and shared our needs, Hebrews 2:11 and 4:15, and He is not ashamed to call the lowliest of His people brothers. The union between Christ and His people is so close that what is done to them is done to Him. This is also what Jesus said to Saul on the Damascus road, 'Why do you persecute Me?' Acts 9:4.

It matters that the King Himself speaks the verdict. The scene never has the angels read out a list or a book open for its evidence; the King addresses each side. And the King who judges is the One about to be judged, since the next chapter begins, 'the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified,' 26:2. The throne and the cross belong to one person. He takes upon Himself the thirst, the nakedness and the prison of the unjust sentence before He pronounces the final verdict.

It is also the King who prepared the kingdom, with His Father, 'from the foundation of the world,' verse 34, and who prepared the fire for the devil, not for human beings. His purpose is to bring people in, not to cast them out.
study.god:
The first thing the chapter shows about God is that He keeps promises, and that He keeps them in His own time. The bridegroom is delayed, the master is gone 'a long time,' and the King comes only at the end. None of this contradicts His faithfulness. The delay is part of the plan, and the same patience that gives time to the foolish virgins to buy oil gives time to the whole world to hear the gospel. God does not hurry because He is not anxious, and He does not forget because He is not limited.

He is a God who gives. 'The kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world,' verse 34, means that the inheritance was planned before anyone could earn it. The talents are given before any service is done. The oil, whatever it is, is the sort of thing a person has to receive. The Father blesses before the Son welcomes, and the whole picture is a generous God who equips and then rewards, so that even the reward is gift upon gift.

He is also a God who judges, and His judgment is not arbitrary. Each of the three scenes shows that the judgment follows what a person has really been all along. The foolish virgins were never ready, the lazy servant never trusted the Master, the goats never loved the King's people. The judgment reveals rather than creates. At the same time, it is serious and it is permanent, since the door is shut, the outer darkness is real, and the verdict is 'eternal.' Nowhere does the text soften that. A God who does not judge would not be good, and a God who did not warn would not be kind.

In verse 41 the fire is 'prepared for the devil and his angels,' and so the passage shows that God did not make hell for people. Those who go there go as those who have taken the devil's side, refusing the one who invited them. The verse closes the question of whether God desires anyone's destruction, and it agrees with Ezekiel 33:11 and with 2 Peter 3:9.

He identifies Himself with the weak. The God of the Old Testament is the one who defends the fatherless and the widow and loves the foreigner, Deuteronomy 10:18, and the Son of God shows what that means by saying that the hungry and the prisoner are Himself. Proverbs 19:17 said that kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, and Jesus makes it concrete.

For worship the chapter asks for the three postures it describes. Wait for Him with joy, because the Bridegroom is coming. Work for Him with trust, because the Master is generous. Serve Him in His people with open hands, because the King is already among them. Each of the three can be done today, and each is a way of saying that the Lord who is coming is also the Lord who is already here.

crossReferences.note: The parable of the virgins echoes the Sermon on the Mount's warning. The foolish virgins call 'Lord, lord' and are answered 'I do not know you,' just as the many who prophesy and cast out demons hear 'I never knew you.' In both places the verdict is about relationship and obedience, not about religious activity.

God as a bridegroom rejoicing over His bride is the prophetic background of the wedding. Isaiah promises that as a young man marries a young woman, so Israel's God will rejoice over His people. Jesus takes the role of the bridegroom, and the joy of the banquet is the joy of that union.

The parable of the minas is the closest parallel to the talents. It was told near Jerusalem to people who thought the kingdom was about to appear, and it adds a rebellion by the nobleman's subjects. Reading it beside Matthew shows that Jesus used the pattern more than once and that the central lesson, faithful use until the master returns, belongs to both.

The LORD speaks of judging 'between one sheep and another, between the rams and the goats,' because the strong have trampled and muddied what the weak needed. Matthew 25 draws on this shepherd's judgment, and the stress on how the weak were treated is the same.

The Son of Man who receives dominion over every nation is the figure on the throne in 25:31. The scene of the nations before Him fills out Daniel's picture of a universal kingdom with the detail of what He will say to each person.

Jesus has already taught that welcoming His messengers is welcoming Him, and that a cup of cold water given to 'one of these little ones' because he is a disciple will not lose its reward. This gives the background for the 'least of these brothers' and shows that the deeds of 25:35-40 are acts of welcome to Christ.

The fast that God chose is to share bread with the hungry, to bring the homeless into your home and to clothe the naked. Three of the six items in Jesus' list appear in the passage, bread for the hungry, shelter for the stranger and clothes for the naked. The prophet says that true worship is mercy to people, and Jesus adds that the people are Himself.

James asks what good it is to tell a hungry, poorly clothed brother to go in peace without supplying his needs. His conclusion, that faith without works is dead, is the lesson of the goats, who said 'Lord' but did not act. Genuine faith shows itself in mercy.

'Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, and He will repay the lender.' Proverbs had already taught that God takes personal notice of mercy to the poor. In Matthew 25, the loan is repaid by the King in person, who says that what was done to the needy was done to Him.

The marriage supper of the Lamb is the final banquet toward which the first parable looks. The bride has made herself ready, in fine linen that is 'the righteous acts of the saints,' and the invitation is a blessing. It shows the same scene as 25:10, with the door open and the feast begun.

Paul says that we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ so that each may receive what is due for deeds done in the body. It is the apostolic statement of what the three parables picture, and Paul draws the same pastoral conclusion, that we make it our aim to please Him.

study.oneStory:
From the first chapters of Genesis, humanity has been given a world to steward and a Lord to walk with. Adam was placed in a garden to work it and keep it, and the first sin was a failure of trust in what the Giver had said. The story that follows is of servants who bury what they were given, of shepherds who feed themselves, and of a people who call God 'Lord' with their lips while their hearts are far from Him. The parables of Matthew 25 are the answer to this long history: a Master has gone away, and when He returns, the question is whether His servants were found faithful.

The chapter answers questions that the Old Testament left open. Who will finally judge? The Son of Man, enthroned. How will the nations be treated? By how they treated the King's people. What will the end look like? A wedding feast for the ready, a joy that the Master shares, and a kingdom that was prepared before the world began. And what about those who would rather not be there? Their destination was never prepared for them, since it was made for the devil and his angels, and they go there by their own choice.

It also sets up what follows. Immediately after the discourse the passion narrative begins, and the same King who sits on the throne in 25:31 is handed over in 26:2. The true Bridegroom is about to be taken away, as He said in 9:15, and the true Servant is about to pour out His life, the single act of faithfulness on which every other faithful servant depends. The hungry, thirsty, naked and imprisoned one who is described in verses 35 and 36 is soon to be all of those things on the cross.

In the story of redemption the parable of the sheep and goats shows how salvation becomes visible. The people of God are those who share the character of their King, a character shown first at the cross and then in the love of His people for one another and for the world. The church lives in the long middle of the story, between the first coming and the second, working with what the Master has given and keeping watch.

The story ends where Revelation ends. The King who judges also welcomes, the door that shut on the unready opens for the faithful, and 'God Himself will be with them,' Revelation 21:3. The kingdom that was prepared from the foundation of the world is received at last, and the tree of life and the river are open again to those who wash their robes, Revelation 22:14. The Garden lost in Genesis is restored as a city, and the joy of the Master is the joy of the redeemed.

quiz.q: What is the main lesson of the parable of the ten virgins?

options.text: Be ready for the Bridegroom's coming with a preparedness that cannot be borrowed at the last moment.
options.note: Verses 10-13 stress readiness that the foolish could not obtain once it was too late.

options.text: Do not fall asleep while waiting for the Lord.
options.note: All ten slept; the difference was the oil, that is, real readiness, not staying awake as such.

options.text: Always share your resources with those who have none.
options.note: The wise could not share the oil; the point is personal readiness, not sharing.

options.text: The Bridegroom will come exactly when expected.
options.note: He was delayed and came at an unexpected hour, hence the call to be ready.

quiz.q: Why was the one-talent servant condemned?

options.text: He buried his master's talent in fear instead of putting it to work.
options.note: Verses 24-27 show his fearful passivity as the fault, not any loss incurred.

options.text: He lost the talent his master had given him.
options.note: He did not lose it; he returned it intact, but he failed to invest it, which was the fault.

options.text: He was given less than the other servants.
options.note: The amount was not the issue; the two-talent servant, with less than the first, was commended.

options.text: He tried to invest but failed to make a profit.
options.note: He did not try at all; he hid the talent in the ground.

quiz.q: On what basis does the King welcome the sheep in the final judgment?

options.text: Their mercy to the least, which revealed their true response to the King Himself.
options.note: Verses 34-40 show deeds of mercy to the least as evidence of belonging to Christ.

options.text: The good deeds by which they earned their place in the kingdom.
options.note: The deeds reveal, rather than earn, salvation; the kingdom was prepared for them from the foundation of the world.

options.text: Their careful avoidance of doing anything wrong.
options.note: The judgment turns on active mercy shown, not merely on avoiding wrong.

options.text: Their success and prosperity in life.
options.note: The criterion is mercy to the needy, not personal success.

quiz.q: What does Jesus teach about the two final destinies?

options.text: The cursed go into eternal punishment and the righteous into eternal life, both everlasting and final.
options.note: Verse 46 sets the two eternal outcomes side by side with the same word.

options.text: The righteous receive eternal life, and the rest simply cease to exist.
options.note: The text names eternal punishment, using the same word as eternal life, not annihilation.

options.text: Everyone is eventually welcomed into the kingdom.
options.note: Jesus clearly separates two groups with two destinies, not universal welcome.

options.text: The destinies are temporary and can later be reversed.
options.note: The judgment is final; both outcomes are described as eternal.

questions: The foolish virgins could not borrow oil at the last minute. What kind of readiness for Christ can only be built now, not scrambled for later?
The fearful servant buried his talent rather than risk it. Where is fear keeping you from investing what God has entrusted to you?
The King is met in the hungry, the stranger, the sick, and the prisoner. Whose need in front of you might actually be an encounter with Christ?
The righteous were surprised they had served the King at all. What would it mean to serve the least without keeping score, simply out of love?
Two eternal destinies hang on this judgment. How does the reality of Christ's return and judgment reshape what you give your life to this week?

translationNotes.note: Some manuscripts add when the Son of Man comes; the command keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour restates the discourse's central charge.
A talent was about twenty years' wages.
The same Greek word, aionios, describes both eternal punishment and eternal life, so the two destinies are presented as equally lasting and final.
